2610.24081v1.title: Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
2610.24081v1.ori_summary: Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.
2610.24081v1.reasoning: Generative engine optimization for LLM answer visibility, not e-commerce ranking or auction mechanisms.

2610.25172v1.title: RemoteANN: A Native Vector Search Engine for Cloud Object Storage
2610.25172v1.authors: Yutong Gou, Silu Huang, Yue Wang, Jianjun Chen, Cheng Long
2610.25172v1.ori_summary: Vector search engines built on cloud object storage have drawn growing attention from both academia and industry. These systems typically adopt a disaggregated storage-compute architecture, persisting the primary vector payload in object stores (e.g., Amazon S3) while retaining compact index metadata on compute nodes. However, conventional vector indexing structures are not natively tailored to the pronounced network latency and per-request access costs of cloud object stores, resulting in network I/O amplification, degraded query throughput, and higher API expenses. To resolve these challenges, we present RemoteANN, a vector search engine explicitly co-designed for cloud object storage across indexing and querying. To mitigate the dominant network I/O bottleneck, RemoteANN couples an Inverted File (IVF) index with RaBitQ quantization, further optimized by inter-cluster and intra-cluster data reordering for improved data locality. Building on this tailored data layout, RemoteANN's query engine combines cluster pruning, fine-grained Range-GET requests, request merging, and local NVMe SSD caching, dramatically reducing discrete storage requests and network transfer volume without sacrificing accuracy. To address the index construction bottleneck, we further develop QGKMeans, which substantially reduces construction latency without compromising clustering quality. Extensive evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that, compared with representative baselines, RemoteANN achieves up to a $5.9\times$ throughput speedup while issuing up to $16.1\times$ fewer object storage requests at 97% target recall.

2610.25172v1.reasoning: Vector search infrastructure paper, not ranking models or auction/mechanism design.

2610.25096v1.title: Toward Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Retail Workflows over Heterogeneous Data Sources
2610.25096v1.authors: Jeonghwan Choi, Jibin Hwang, Hayoon Park, Hyeonjae Cheon, Hwanjun Song
2610.25096v1.ori_summary: Enterprise retail workflows require agents to chain evidence across heterogeneous sources, from structured product and order records to unstructured inquiries and reviews, yet existing agentic RAG benchmarks rarely capture this challenge. To enable controlled evaluation of such workflows, we introduce RetailBridge, a compositional retail benchmark built from persona-driven simulations. Its questions are constructed by linking entities and intermediate answers across heterogeneous sources, requiring agents to identify the relevant sources, carry evidence between them, and produce a grounded answer. To systematically evaluate LLMs on these retail workflows, we develop RetailRAG, a retail-aware framework equipped with auto-schema briefing, source-routed plan chaining, and diagnostic plan revision. On RetailBridge, evaluating ten LLM backbones with RetailRAG reveals multi-source chaining as the dominant bottleneck across providers and model scales, suggesting that reliable retail agents require explicit cross-source orchestration rather than scaling alone. 2610.25779v1.title: OpenSaC: A Python Library for Search as Code in Deep Research Agents
2610.25779v1.authors: Qi Liu, Jiaxin Mao, Fengbin Zhu, Tat-Seng Chua, Ji-Rong Wen
2610.25779v1.ori_summary: Deep research agents investigate complex questions through iterative search, source examination, and evidence synthesis. A conventional workflow alternates reasoning with individual search and reading actions. Search as Code introduces a new paradigm: agents write programs that compose search, source reading, reranking, model calls, and local processing, returning selected observations for further reasoning. To support this workflow in existing coding agents, we present OpenSaC, an open-source Python library with a companion Search as Code skill. Configurable capability interfaces let agents combine these operations while retaining evidence for inspection and reuse. Compared with standard Codex using its built-in web search, the OpenSaC configuration uses less execution time and fewer model tokens on BrowseComp and WideSearch, with higher accuracy on BrowseComp and slightly lower row F1 on WideSearch. We aim to lower the barrier to adopting Search as Code and provide an open foundation for community development and transparent research on deep research agents.

2610.25678v1.title: Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
2610.25678v1.authors: Seokwon Jung, Yerang Kim, Yejin Kim, Alexander Rubinstein, Arnas Uselis, Sangwoo Park, Seong Joon Oh, Sangdoo Yun
2610.25678v1.ori_summary: Many scientific advances come from cross-pollination, carrying an idea from one field over to a problem in another. We study cross-pollination retrieval, the problem of identifying transferable ideas across research fields, and introduce CPR-Dataset, a large-scale dataset constructed by mining cross-topic citations. Its evaluation split CPR-eval has 1,300 queries in 26 fields, and its training split CPR-train has 10,573 pairs. On CPR-eval, the best of eleven existing retrievers reaches a Recall@10 of only 0.26, whereas an LLM reranker reaches 0.81. Standard contrastive fine-tuning on CPR-train raises Recall@10 to as high as 0.70. The gain carries over to domains held out from training and to analogy and reasoning-intensive retrieval. On AnaloBench, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 33% over the untrained retriever, whereas training on three existing retrieval datasets lowers it. On BRIGHT, it raises nDCG@10 by up to 70%, more than twice the gain from those datasets. CPR-Dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/CPR-Dataset, and the code at https://github.com/SeokwonJung-Jay/Cross-Pollination-Retrieval.

2610.26831v1.title: AGR: Agentic Generative Retrieval with Tool-Augmented Search
2610.26831v1.authors: Ming Yang, Yaqi Yin, Zhibo Wang, Xiaoze Jiang, Jingwei Zhuo, Chao Zhang, Quanzhi Zhu, Weiguo Zheng, Liang Zeng, Yunfeng Zhao, Jiaqiang Liu, Kefeng Wang, Yupeng Huang, Kaiqiao Zhan, Xuanping Li
2610.26831v1.ori_summary: Large-scale search and recommendation systems derive much of their retrieval quality from rich, heterogeneous features, yet existing generative retrieval (GR) methods struggle to exploit such feature ecosystems efficiently. Static feature injection either encodes all available signals or places them according to predetermined schemes, increasing serving cost and introducing irrelevant or conflicting evidence. More fundamentally, existing methods cannot adaptively determine when a feature is needed, which feature to select, or where it should influence hierarchical Semantic ID (SID) generation. We propose Agentic Generative Retrieval (AGR), a tool-augmented paradigm that interleaves SID generation with on-demand feature acquisition. Conditioned on the request and decoded SID prefix, AGR decides whether to invoke a tool, which feature to acquire, and where its observation should influence subsequent decoding, thereby steering generation toward feature-consistent SID branches. To supervise this behavior, we construct tool-augmented trajectories based on feature applicability and information gain along the SID hierarchy, and train the model through SID pretraining followed by tool-augmented fine-tuning. Experiments on an industrial dataset and three public benchmarks, together with an online A/B test, consistently demonstrate the effectiveness of AGR.

2610.24481v1.title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
2610.24481v1.authors: Jiang Wu, Yutong Song, Hongbo Wang, Guanghe Cao, Jeff Liang
2610.24481v1.ori_summary: Language models can make personalized recommendations from rich item content, user history, and feedback. However, evaluating many candidates with full-text inputs incurs substantial online computation and limits serving throughput. We introduce DuoLM, a framework for fast and effective personalized recommendation that integrates a compact recommendation model with an efficient serving runtime. An encoder LLM learns compact item representations for offline reuse, while a personalized ranker LLM combines them with user history and feedback for recommendation. We train both models end to end with recommendation supervision and teacher distillation. The runtime further accelerates inference through virtual token IDs for embedding access, shared history computation, and CUDA Graph replay. Benchmark results show that our framework achieves recommendation quality comparable to that of the expert teacher model. On a single H100, it delivers approximately 26,400 candidate scores per second, about $60\times$ the throughput of the teacher served with vLLM and automatic prefix caching.

2610.26339v1.title: Large-Scale Biomedical RAG: Corpus Scaling, Document Representation, and Efficiency Trade-offs
2610.26339v1.authors: Adrián Sánchez-Freire, Gonzalo Pérez-Gómez, Aitziber Atutxa, Ander Barrena
2610.26339v1.ori_summary: We present a controlled, large-scale evaluation of how corpus scale, document representation, and reranking affect the effectiveness and efficiency of biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. Retrieval collections were progressively expanded while retaining the relevant source documents, enabling consistent comparisons across corpus sizes. We compared abstract, flat full-text, and hierarchical full-text representations across first-stage retrieval, reranking, and end-to-end multiple-choice question answering. Configurations selected on development data were evaluated on five external biomedical benchmarks and a held-out test set, while retrieval latency and index storage were measured to quantify operational cost. Performance patterns observed with small or controlled collections did not consistently persist as collections grew, and the usefulness of reranking depended on the corpus and retrieval setting. RAG improved three of four model configurations across the external benchmarks, with mean gains of up to 9.6 percentage points, and improved all four configurations on the held-out test set by 10.2-30.3 points. Abstract retrieval performed best when reference evidence was abstract-aligned, whereas full-text representations were generally more effective when richer evidence was needed. Hierarchical representation matched or outperformed flat full-text retrieval in most end-to-end comparisons while requiring 67% fewer indexed units and 44-56% less storage. These findings show that corpus scale should be treated as an explicit evaluation variable in biomedical RAG, and that the most appropriate design depends on evidence format, model behavior, and operational constraints.

2610.25413v1.title: Weakly Supervised Adaptation of Scientific Embeddings for Exploratory Literature Mapping
2610.25413v1.authors: Roman Neruda, Petra Vidnerová, Jiří Šejnoha, Jakub Mihálik, Tomáš Marvan
2610.25413v1.ori_summary: Scientific document embeddings such as SPECTER2 are optimized for retrieval over large, heterogeneous corpora. On a small specialized corpus their similarity distributions can become highly compressed, which limits their usefulness for exploratory literature mapping. We study whether weakly supervised in-domain adaptation, using only metadata already available in open citation databases, changes this geometry. On ArtCon, a curated corpus of 704 publications on artificial and machine consciousness, we adapt the SPECTER2 proximity model with a lightweight LoRA adapter trained on positive pairs derived from bibliographic coupling in OpenAlex, using no manually annotated similarity labels. We compare the adapted embeddings with lexical (TF-IDF), citation-based (bibliographic coupling) and generic semantic (SPECTER2) representations under thresholded, fixed-density and symmetric k-nearest-neighbour graph constructions. Adaptation substantially decompresses the similarity distribution (mean pairwise cosine similarity 0.9104 to 0.8663, standard deviation 0.0259 to 0.0594) and yields graphs with markedly higher Louvain modularity and better connectivity than the base encoder under matched edge and neighbourhood budgets. The effect is stable across all three graph constructions and is therefore not an artefact of a single sparsification choice. We report this as a case study on one corpus, and we are explicit about what it does not establish: the clustering indices used here are computed against community labels derived from each representation's own similarity graph, so they measure internal geometric self-consistency rather than agreement with an external topical ground truth, and adaptation and evaluation use the same documents. Evaluation against independent labels, on held-out documents, and against geometric controls is ongoing work.

2610.25371v1.title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
2610.25371v1.ori_summary: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.

2610.25221v1.title: When Semantics Fall Short: Persona-Guided Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Large Language Models
2610.25221v1.authors: Jundong Chen, Honglei Zhang, Shuai An, Enneng Yang, Han Yu
2610.25221v1.ori_summary: Cross-domain sequential recommendation (CDSR) alleviates data sparsity by transferring user behaviors across domains. Recent advances increasingly leverage large language models (LLMs) to bridge domains through global item semantics. However, this paradigm is inherently limited by two issues: I. semantic domain isolation, where item semantics remain domain-specific and hinder transferable modeling, and II. semantic-behavior inconsistency, where local semantic relations are more consistent with behavioral transitions, whereas such consistency often breaks down globally across domains. To this end, we propose PerCDR, an LLM-enhanced CDSR framework that shifts the focus from global semantic bridging to persona-guided behavioral modeling. Specifically, PerCDR leverages LLM-inferred personas to globally guide transferable cross-domain behavioral patterns, while exploiting local semantic relations to enhance intra-domain behavioral modeling, followed by domain preference adaptation for recommendation refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of PerCDR and validate its effectiveness.

2610.24822v1.authors: Omar El Bachyr, Laura Maria Bernardy, Saad Ezzini, Jacques Klein, Tegawendé F. Bissyandé, Charles Mont'e, Anas Zilali, Ulrick Ble, Anne Goujon

2610.24107v1.title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
2610.24107v1.authors: Yi Fang, Gaurav Srivastava, Zhenyu Bi, Sirui Ding, Xuan Wang
2610.24107v1.ori_summary: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.

2610.24030v1.title: When Does Evidence-Graph Structure Predict Answer Correctness? Label-Free Abstention for Structured Retrieval
2610.24030v1.ori_summary: Retrieval systems return scored answers, but a high score does not show that an answer should be trusted. The proposed training-free abstention method applies the boundary cut to the selected evidence in an evidence graph. The signal is the weighted cut between selected and unselected candidates and requires no correctness labels or confidence-model training. On MemoryAgentBench (MAB) FactConsolidation multi-hop, with unresolved queries ranked last for every selector, it raises area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.736 for the best score baseline to 0.785 (+0.049, 95% CI [+0.008, +0.092]); under the native evaluation, where score baselines keep their unresolved values, the gap is +0.108. A zero-cut subset contains 71 of 400 queries at 100% observed precision. In this pipeline, the subset corresponds to structural closure; controlled analyses attribute much of the remaining separation to resolution status, with little benefit from continuous edge weights. Across external benchmarks, usefulness varies with graph construction, edge semantics, and relation; typed structure alone does not ensure useful confidence. A supervised gradient-boosted selector achieves 0.814 versus the boundary cut's 0.785 when the retrieval stack matches. These findings provide empirical guidance for using available evidence graphs for lightweight, auditable post-retrieval abstention without additional model inference.

2610.24341v1.title: Optimal Fusion Weights Form Intervals, Not Points: A Latency-Aware Study of Query-Adaptive WRRF
2610.24341v1.authors: Iris Ma, Zahra Shekarchi, Stuart Mcilroy, Mahtab Farrokh, Fattane Zarrinkalam, Joel Stremmel
2610.24341v1.ori_summary: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is widely used to combine sparse and dense retrievers in hybrid information retrieval, but a critical limitation is that it assigns a fixed, uniform weight to each retriever regardless of the query. Query-aware methods treat the per-query optimal weight as a single point, an assumption whose empirical validity has not been examined. We present an empirical study of eight dynamic fusion weight prediction strategies across four datasets and four sparse--dense retriever pairs. When we compare these approaches to static fusion and a per-query oracle that bounds achievable performance, several findings emerge. First, the per-query optimal fusion weight is typically an interval rather than a point. Queries can have multiple optimal intervals, and these can take on a variety of shapes. Second, 74 of 128 dynamic fusion methods tested were significantly better than standard RRF after false discovery rate correction. Third, dynamic fusion methods exhibit differing quality and latency characteristics that should be considered when choosing an appropriate fusion method. To address this last finding, we present a tiered decision framework that maps practitioner constraints, dataset properties, label availability, hardware, and latency budget to an appropriate method class. We release the code for our experiments at https://github.com/thomsonreuters/query-based-rrf.

2610.25575v1.title: Benchmark for Structured Retrieval-Augmented Generation in Perovskite Photovoltaics
2610.25575v1.authors: Qiwei Han, Chi Zhou, Gaoxiang Yuan

2610.25373v1.title: MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data
2610.25373v1.authors: Sen Gao, Yongan Li, Han Chen, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich, Shixuan Sun
2610.25373v1.ori_summary: Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive. Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01% when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.
2610.25373v1.reasoning: Benchmark for agent memory over evolving data; unrelated to ranking/auction mechanisms.

2610.25323v1.title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
2610.25323v1.authors: Tianyi Hu, Bhavyajeet Singh, Niket Tandon, Akhil Arora
2610.25323v1.ori_summary: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. 2610.22381v1.ori_summary: When a fact becomes harder to elicit from a language model, has the model lost it, or has it merely become less accessible? 2610.23255v1.title: Sample, Mix, or Verify? Allocating Test-Time Compute under Imperfect Verifiers
2610.23255v1.ori_summary: A common way to make language models and agents more accurate is to spend more compute at inference time: generate many candidate solutions and submit the one a verifier prefers. Success then requires that some candidate is correct and that the verifier picks it. The first grows predictably with the number of samples; the second does not, because real verifiers (unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, reward models) accept wrong answers, reject right ones, and make correlated mistakes. With a fixed budget, a practitioner must decide how many samples to draw, which models to draw them from, and how much to spend on verification, and today these choices are made by rules of thumb. We introduce SPLIT, which makes them from a small labelled pilot. It rests on an exact formula for the probability of submitting a correct answer under accept/reject and top-score selection that accounts for varying task difficulty, blind spots shared across models, and correlated repeated verifier calls. SPLIT fits the formula by empirical Bayes and uses it to plan budgets on unseen tasks. Across seven benchmarks spanning math, science QA, code and software-engineering agents, 26 models, 175 agent systems and six kinds of real verifiers, all from public releases, SPLIT lands within 0.02-0.8 percentage points of the best allocation in hindsight, while every fixed rule we test loses at least 2.5 points in some setting. Regret depends only on how well SPLIT ranks configurations, and it stays near-optimal under compute, price and latency costs and online. The formula also explains when asking more LLM judges lowers precision. As a forecaster far beyond the pilot, SPLIT beats power-law fitting when the verifier caps success, and we report where it loses.

2610.23149v1.title: Can AI interview? Comparing AI-led to Human-led Chat Interviews

2610.22467v1.title: Progressive Misalignment Can Emerge from Benign Recursive Self-Distillation
2610.22467v1.authors: Karim Abdel Sadek, Federico Di Gennaro, Fanny Yang
2610.22467v1.ori_summary: Training models on their own outputs has attracted widespread attention as a possible route to advance AI capabilities. 2610.23625v1.title: PresenceBench: An Exploratory Evaluation of Large Language Model Adaptation to User State
2610.23625v1.authors: Peña Arroyo Gallego, Mauro Ruiz Moreno, Alejandro Acien, Sergio Romero-Tapiador, Teresa Arroyo-Gallego

2610.23257v1.title: Reasoning Models Can Control Their Chains of Thought When They Tell Themselves To
2610.23257v1.authors: Uriel Dolev, Idan Schwartz, Yoav Goldberg

2610.22724v1.authors: Tong Guo, Teng Ye, Yutong Xie, Qiaozhu Mei

2610.22599v1.title: Can LLMs predict the outcomes of machine learning experiments?
2610.22599v1.authors: Ayush Bansal, Aldo Pareja, Sean Klein, Serge Didenko, Artem Lukoianov

2610.22455v1.title: High prevalence of antagonizing rhetoric in trending topics on Twitter/X

2610.23818v1.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
2610.23818v1.authors: Chiatzen Wang, Bill Xu, Haochen Gu, Hongyang Zhang
2610.23818v1.ori_summary: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. 2610.25608v1.title: Hardness Amplification for Approximate Nash Equilibrium with Constantly Many Players

2610.26535v1.ori_summary: The metric distortion framework asks voting rules to elect a candidate close to the voters using only their rankings. 2610.26772v1.title: Tight Inapproximability for Generalized Circuits
2610.26772v1.ori_summary: Generalized circuits are a fundamental tool for establishing PPAD-hardness and membership of approximate equilibrium problems. Despite their importance, the complexity of finding approximate solutions has remained unresolved for a wide range of approximation parameters. Specifically, we prove that $\varepsilon$-GCircuit is PPAD-complete for every constant $0<\varepsilon<1/6$, even when restricted to four gate types, and polynomial-time solvable for every constant $\varepsilon\ge1/6$. We establish polynomial-time solvability of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-GCircuit for every constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $δ>1/5$, and of the fan-out-one formulations of $δ$-Pure-Circuit for every constant $δ>1/8$. These results follow from a decomposition theorem for directed graphs of maximum in-degree two and establish that the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture cannot be true for the aforementioned values of $\varepsilon$ and $δ$, unless PPAD = P. To showcase the contribution of our positive results, we apply them to a variety of problems in algorithmic game theory, including public goods games, financial networks, Bayesian, polymatrix, and graphical games, and obtain improved approximation guarantees.

2610.24697v1.title: Blockchain Participation Games with Upfront Contribution Commitment
2610.24697v1.ori_summary: Blockchain participation games model costly entry, random selection, and threshold success; their retraction variants charge completion costs only to selected contributors. We study committee tasks requiring operators to reserve computing or communication capacity before assignment, so preparation costs are incurred even when capacity remains unused. The results distinguish free-riding on public value from registration that earns rewards without productive commitment; more frequently selected users can choose bare registration while less frequently selected users contribute. Our main result characterizes every homogeneous minimum-outlay scheme supporting full contribution, where every user commits, as a Nash equilibrium. When positive rewards are required, these schemes form a line segment. There is always an optimum with no registration reward. It eliminates every equilibrium containing bare registrants at minimum outlay while retaining the full-contribution equilibrium; threshold-coordination failures may remain. Under heterogeneous selection, a two-user instance has a unique optimum using both rewards, cheaper than every zero-registration-reward scheme supporting full contribution. Finally, if full contribution is a positive-welfare social optimum, the homogeneous zero-registration-reward design attains price of stability one. 2610.23860v1.title: Modeling Human Behavior in the Prisoner's Dilemma with Large Language Models
2610.23860v1.ori_summary: The Prisoner's Dilemma has long served as a foundational framework for studying human decision-making and cooperative outcomes across social scenarios, yet human behavior consistently deviates from predictions of fully rational economic theory. Previous works have studied human and LLM outcomes in the Prisoner's Dilemma; however, these studies have lacked at least one key feature: a memory component for LLM agents, accessible open-source models, or comparison against empirical human data. This project investigates whether open-source LLMs, TII Falcon 7B Instruct, Google Gemma 7B, Meta Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Microsoft Phi Mini MoE Instruct, and Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, can model human cooperation patterns in repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games, while examining how an LLM's knowledge that its opponent will be shuffled affects its decisions. Using a standardized prompting framework, we simulated interactions in two trial types: a fixed-partner setting where both agents retain memory, and a shuffled-partner setting where a memory-enabled agent, informed that its opponent changes across rounds, interacts with a memoryless agent. For each trial, we measured cooperation rates over 100 rounds and 10-round increments and compared them to human data from Montero-Porras et al. (2022). Under both frameworks, all LLMs differed from the human cooperation rate. Open-source LLMs generally over-cooperated relative to humans, particularly in the shuffled framework, where human cooperation averaged 28.5% while several models exceeded 80%. Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct showed deterministic tendencies, while Phi-mini-MoE-Instruct displayed greater variability and briefly approximated human rates. These findings suggest that LLMs have potential as behavioral simulation agents and provide a benchmark across two interaction environments, although open-source models are not yet reliable substitutes for human participants.

2610.24792v1.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
2610.24792v1.ori_summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

2610.25188v1.title: Strategy recovery for Mean-Payoff Games is as hard as solving them from scratch
2610.25188v1.ori_summary: Mean-Payoff Games (MPGs) form an interesting family of deterministic, infinite-duration, zero-sum, turn-based games played by two players on a finite weighted directed graph. The goal of the players is to minimize, respectively maximize, the $\textit{limiting average}$ of the costs of the edges on an infinite path constructed by the two players. The complexity of solving MPGs is a long-standing open question. The decision problem associated with these games is known to be in $\text{NP}\cap \text{co-NP}$, and even $\text{UP}\cap \text{co-UP}$, yet the problem is not known to be in $\text{P}$. This is one of the simplest combinatorial problems with such a status. A full solution of an MPG gives the $\textit{value}$ of each vertex of the game, along with a pair of $\textit{optimal strategies}$ for the two players. (Each player has a succinct $\textit{positional}$ optimal strategy.) The problem of finding optimal strategies for the players given the values of all vertices is known as the $\textit{strategy recovery}$ problem. We describe a simple reduction from the problem of solving MPGs to the strategy recovery problem for MPGs. This shows that the strategy recovery problem for MPGs is essentially as hard as solving MPGs from scratch, i.e., without knowing the values. The reduction uses simple $\textit{game transformations}$ and simple $\textit{self-reducibility}$ and $\textit{peeling}$ arguments. This answers a question of Andersson and Miltersen. Mamino obtained a similar result for $\textit{stochastic}$ games with a limiting average objective, but his technique does not extend to deterministic games such as MPGs. We go one step further and show that finding an optimal strategy for one of the players of an MPG remains hard even if an optimal strategy of the second player, and hence all the values, are known.
